sentences.text: Trilophosuchus was an extinct genus of crocodilian belonging to the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
Its common name translates to triple-crested crocodile, referring to three parallel ridges on the skull table of this short, high-headed animal with relatively large eyes.
The snout was thought to be very robust, featuring a trapezoid cross-section just before the eyes.
The skull measures only 79 mm from the back of the head to the front of the rostrum, indicating a very small size.
This species is unusual among mekosuchines and crocodilians for having a short snout and an arboreal lifestyle, unlike its relatives which were terrestrial.
The holotype skull, considered one of the best-preserved fossil crocodilians from Australia despite missing the snout, was uncovered in 1985 during an excavation by the University of New South Wales.
Paul Willis of the University of Sydney erected the genus in 1993 and named it in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.
The species name rackhami honors Alan Rackham Senior, a supporter of the Riversleigh excavations.
Evidence of skull bone fusion and surface sculpting indicates that the holotype specimen was an adult when it died.
Researchers suggest that Trilophosuchus was a dwarf species exhibiting juvenile-like traits due to paedomorphy rather than being an immature individual.
The short snout contrasts with the long snouts of large carnivorous crocodilians, suggesting Trilophosuchus restricted its diet to small prey analogous to small agamas and iguanas.
It may have consumed fish, turtles, snakes, and small mammals, all of which have been found at Riversleigh.
Trilophosuchus is unusual among mekosuchines and crocodilians in general for having a short, high snout and an arboreal lifestyle.
Only a single species, Trilophosuchus rackhami, has been described for the genus.
Despite resembling early crocodyliforms, Trilophosuchus is classified as an advanced crocodilian.
Trilophosuchus belongs to the subfamily Mekosuchinae, a group of endemic Australian and New Caledonian crocodiles.
Fossils of Trilophosuchus have been found at the Ringtail Site in north-western Queensland, dating to the Miocene epoch, approximately 20 million years ago.
Additional remains found at the older Hiatus Site extend the known range of Trilophosuchus into the Oligocene, between 27.3 and 11.63 million years ago.
The fossil range of Trilophosuchus spans from the Early to Middle Miocene.

The Ringtail Site where Trilophosuchus fossils were found preserves evidence of a pool in a forested karst terrain that included aquatic animals like lungfish, turtles, and the extinct platypus Obdurodon dicksoni.
It is debated whether the Oligocene material found at the Hiatus Site represents a second species of Trilophosuchus or simply age-related variation.
A 2018 study by Stein et al. placed Trilophosuchus as a basal form related to Ultrastenos, a result later deemed irregular due to problematic taxa.
It is unclear how Trilophosuchus and Mekosuchus sanderi differed in their ecology despite both being thought to be terrestrial animals.

Because Trilophosuchus is similar in appearance to M. inexpectatus, it has frequently been suggested that it was also arboreal, though Mekosuchus inexpectatus had limb bone structures compatible with climbing while there is no evidence that Trilophosuchus had climbing abilities.
